rep_lodsb · Oct 31, 2026

All the values are divisible by 8, so it could do it like this:

    cmp  eax,40
    ja   <return 0>
    test eax,7
    jnz  <return 0>
    jmp  JumpTable[rax]

LarsKrimi · Oct 31, 2026

Okay. Good point, that is quite a bit shorter than I first thought of

A rough benchmark of a version of that against the original shows it to be close to twice as fast for unpredictable input with GCC (4.5 ns vs 2.72 ns) on my old machine. With predictable input where x values often are the same the original version is quicker

    int sparse_8_jump(int x, int val) {
        unsigned int idx = (unsigned int)x >> 3;
        if (idx > 5)
            return 0;
        if (x & 7)
            return 0;
        
        switch (idx) {
            case 0:
                return f0(val);
            case 1:
                return f1(val);
            case 2:
                return f2(val);
            case 3:
                return f3(val);
            case 5:
                return f4(val);
            default:
                return 0;
        }
    }

Findecanor · Oct 31, 2026

That optimisation is simply missing.

Each `jmp` to f0..fX is an optimisation of a `call` and a `ret`, and probably done in a separate pass after the switch-case code has already been expanded.

The `mov edi, esi` at the top of the function is also an optimisation, most likely done during the register allocation pass. This was only possible because all functions take the same value in the same register. Otherwise, there would probably have been also a `mov` before each of the calls.
